title: Data preprocessing techniques for classification without discrimination
abstract: Recently, the following Discrimination-Aware Classification Problem was introduced: Suppose we are given training data that exhibit unlawful discrimination; e.g., toward sensitive attributes such as gender or ethnicity. The task is to learn a classifier that optimizes accuracy, but does not have this discrimination in its predictions on test data. This problem is relevant in many settings, such as when the data are generated by a biased decision process or when the sensitive attribute serves as a proxy for unobserved features. In this paper, we concentrate on the case with only one binary sensitive attribute and a two-class classification problem. We first study the theoretically optimal trade-off between accuracy and non-discrimination for pure classifiers. Then, we look at algorithmic solutions that preprocess the data to remove discrimination before a classifier is learned. We survey and extend our existing data preprocessing techniques, being suppression of the sensitive attribute, massaging the dataset by changing class labels, and reweighing or resampling the data to remove discrimination without relabeling instances. These preprocessing techniques have been implemented in a modified version of Weka and we present the results of experiments on real-life data.

claims.text: Removing the sensitive attribute from a dataset does not always remove discrimination due to correlations with remaining attributes.
Applying Preferential Sampling with a J48 base learner on the Census Income dataset reduces discrimination from 16.48% to 3.32%.
Applying Preferential Sampling with a J48 base learner on the Census Income dataset reduces classification accuracy from 86.05% to 84.30%.
For deterministic classifiers that do not utilize scoring rankers, lowering discrimination results in a strictly linear decrease in accuracy.

limitations.text: The formalizations and techniques presented are concentrated on the case with only one binary sensitive attribute and a binary classification problem.
Massaging is intrusive because it changes the ground-truth class labels of training data objects.
Reweighing cannot be directly applied to classifier learning algorithms that do not support weighted instances.
Naive attribute suppression fails to prevent indirect discrimination due to proxy attributes that correlate with the sensitive attribute.

future_work.text: Extend non-discrimination constraints to conditional non-discrimination constraints where correlation with the sensitive attribute is allowed if explainable by neutral attributes.
Extend preprocessing techniques to support multi-class classification problems and sensitive attributes with more than two values.
Develop techniques to handle multiple sensitive attributes simultaneously, such as combinations of gender and ethnicity.
Adapt discrimination-aware preprocessing techniques to handle numerical sensitive attributes.

methodologies.name: Massaging
methodologies.description: A data preprocessing technique that relabels borderline promotion and demotion candidates identified by a ranking classifier to eliminate discrimination from the training set.

methodologies.name: Reweighing
methodologies.description: A data preprocessing technique that assigns weights to training tuples based on expected versus observed probabilities under statistical independence without altering class labels.
conditions: base learner must support instance weights

methodologies.name: Preferential Sampling
methodologies.description: A sampling technique that prioritizes duplicating or removing borderline objects identified by a ranker to achieve expected non-discriminatory group sizes.

methodologies.name: Uniform Sampling
methodologies.description: A sampling technique that applies uniform stratified sampling with replacement across four sensitive-attribute and class combinations to reach non-discriminatory group sizes.
